_note: The archetype as such: Jung's epistemological keystone. The model (CW9i ¶6), the name (CW8 ¶270-275), the instinct's side (CW8 ¶339, ¶277, CW16 ¶208), the empty form and its plurality (CW9i ¶155, ¶99), and the seminar's bluntest statement of it. Quotations are placed by the corpus (scripts/theory-pages.mjs); nothing is typed.
line: Where Jung defines the archetype as such and sets it beside the word's ancestry, the instincts and typical situations: CW9i, CW8, CW16 and the Dream Analysis seminar of 1930.

sections.title: The model
sections.line: CW9i ¶6 and ¶155, and the Dream Analysis seminar of 12 March 1930: the archetype called a hypothetical and irrepresentable model, empty and purely formal, perfectly indescribable.

quotes.quote: The archetype as such is a hypothetical and irrepresentable model
The archetype in itself is empty and purely formal
Any archetype is really perfectly indescribable, something perfectly empty, but capable of assimilating a certain kind of material of tremendous variation.

sections.title: The name
sections.line: CW8 ¶275, in Instinct and the Unconscious (1919): Jung names Augustine as the source of the idea of the archetype; the vault records ¶270 of that essay as his first use of the term.

quotes.quote: from whom I have borrowed the idea of the archetype
down to Malebranche and Bacon, still stands on a Platonic footing in this respect.

sections.title: The instinct's side
sections.line: CW8 ¶339 (The Structure of the Psyche, 1927), CW8 ¶277 and a passage of CW16: the archetypes set beside the instincts.

quotes.quote: archetypes are simply the forms which the instincts assume
as the self-portrait of the instinct, in exactly the same way as consciousness is an inward perception of the objective
an instinct is always and inevitably coupled with something like a philosophy of life

sections.title: As many as situations
sections.line: CW9i ¶99: how many archetypes there are, in Jung's words.

quotes.quote: as many archetypes as there are typical situations
